transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-28 15:42 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya, Liam (Redwood); Priya, Daniel, Aisha (Ember Finance)
Links shared: https://redwood.example.com/security/ember-finance (security pack), https://redwood.example.com/console-demo (console GIF)

Summary:
Quick demo of request-storage controls in Console + API examples for selective telemetry ejection, PII suppression rules, and ephemeral request storage. Covered KMS/HSM integration options and enterprise retention defaults. Agreed to spin up pilot org with ephemeral request storage and run latency benchmarks.

Topics covered:
- Console toggles: request storage on/off/ephemeral, retention windows, manual ejection
- Redaction profiles: regex, ML PII detectors (heuristic), and token-level masking
- API flags: store_request=false, pii_policy=standard, telemetry_eject_rule=prefix-match
- KMS integration and audit logs
- Pilot next steps and benchmarks

Action items (recap): see metadata action_items above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you squeezing us in, uh Priya, Daniel, Aisha, glad to meet you. Liam and I will run through the console toggles and then swing to the API examples.
[00:18] Priya Singh: Thanks Maya, excited to see how we can limit logs — compliance is the big ask, we need to make sure nothing sensitive leaves our environment.
[00:24] Liam O'Connor: Totally, we'll show two patterns: ephemeral request storage which never lands on disk after inference completes, and selective telemetry ejection where we proactively strip fields before persisting.
[00:36] Daniel Kwan: Quick Q up front — is the request_storage flag per-tenant or per-route? We have mixed workloads; some routes can log for debugging.
[00:45] Liam O'Connor: Good question — you can set at three levels: org-default, route-level override, or on individual API calls with header overrides (x-redwood-store: false). So you can keep debug routes logging while customer-facing ones are ephemeral.
[00:58] Aisha Roberts: When you say "ephemeral" what's the retention window, like zero or 24 hours? Our legal wants zero persistent copy.
[01:07] Liam O'Connor: Ephemeral is zero-persistent by default — the payload is held in memory and KV cache but not written to request storage. We do have an "ephemeral+buffer" mode for short replay debugging (configurable to 1 hour). That mode still encrypts in transit and in-mem.
[01:23] Priya Singh: Ok, good. Also need to hear about redaction — we have PHI tokens and account numbers, want deterministic masking.
[01:30] Maya Chen: We'll demo the console redaction profiles — regex-based rules you can upload, plus our ML PII detector which tags tokens and can either mask or eject the whole field.
[01:38] [00:01:40] Speaker 4: (low audio) - can you show an example?
[01:45] Liam O'Connor: Sure — switching to screen. (brief pause) So here is the Console > Data Controls tab, you can see the default profile called "Redwood Standard". You can create a custom profile and add rules. For Ember I'd suggest: regex for account numbers, ML detector for names/dates, and a tokenization ejection pattern for anything that looks like SSN.
[02:12] Daniel Kwan: When you say "tokenization ejection" do you mean we drop tokens pre-inference or after inference? We need to preserve prompt context sometimes.
[02:22] Liam O'Connor: We have two modes: pre-token ejection — remove tokens before they hit the model (safer for PII but loses context), and KV-level mask — keep a masked placeholder in the prompt so model still sees structure, e.g., replace with [PII_REDACTED]. You choose per-rule.
[02:39] Priya Singh: Can the mask be reversible for our SREs (like hashed + lookup) — or is it one-way?
[02:46] Liam O'Connor: It's configurable: you can choose irreversible redaction, reversible hashed token stored in a KMS-protected store, or ephemeral reversible only within a bounded TTL. Reversible requires explicit KMS permissions and audit logging.
[02:59] Aisha Roberts: Audit logging is critical — we need proof we redacted. Does your audit show the original or only the action?
[03:06] Maya Chen: Audit logs show metadata and the rule that triggered the redaction, but the original plaintext can be redacted from logs depending on your compliance profile — if you enable reversible storage, the original is gated behind KMS access and recorded in the audit.
[03:20] Priya Singh: Okay that's helpful. Walk us through an API example — we want to implement minimal changes client-side.
[03:26] Liam O'Connor: On the API side you have request flags. Example cURL: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -H "x-redwood-store: false" -d '{"input": "..."}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate. Also you can pass "pii_policy": "strict" in the JSON to apply server-side ejection.
[03:46] Daniel Kwan: Is there a latency cost for server-side PII detection? We care about 95th percentile latency.
[03:52] Liam O'Connor: There is some modest overhead — the ML PII detector runs in a streaming pass; we optimize with batching. For most short requests it's ~10-30ms extra; for larger body text it may be higher. We'll include perf numbers in the benchmark but you can pre-tag on client if latency is critical.
[04:09] Priya Singh: Does the detector run on Dedicated or Private in the same way?
[04:13] Liam O'Connor: Yes — runtime parity across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. On Private you can deploy the detector in your VPC and route calls locally; the console still controls the ruleset via your private control plane.
[04:25] Aisha Roberts: Our legal asked about encryption at rest for the temporary buffer. You mentioned KMS earlier. Is that customer-managed?
[04:32] Maya Chen: For Dedicated and Private you can use customer-managed KMS/HSM. Hosted supports Redwood-managed KMS with options to bring your own key in enterprise plans.
[04:41] [00:04:41] Priya Singh: Any SOC 2 or ISO docs for this?
[04:44] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll send the SOC2 package. It's the first action item. Also our compliance pack includes a sample configuration showing how to disable request storage and still get metrics.
[04:55] Daniel Kwan: Metrics? If we turn off storage, can we still get per-model latency and cost metrics?
[05:01] Liam O'Connor: Yes — telemetry metrics are aggregated and de-identified. We provide token-level cost, latency percentiles, and error counts without storing full request payloads. You can enable metrics-only mode — we store headers and timing but not request body.
[05:14] Priya Singh: That sounds promising. How do you handle third-party integrations — we use Datadog and SIEM tools.
[05:20] Maya Chen: We emit structured telemetry events and you can choose to route them to your monitoring. The events are schema-controlled so no PII fields by default; any custom links back to original request require explicit consent and storage toggles.
[05:34] Aisha Roberts: Talk to me about deletion requests — if a user asks to delete their data, can you guarantee removal from all logs?
[05:41] Liam O'Connor: Yes, Redwood has an ejection API: POST /orgs/{id}/eject with selectors. It runs a targeted purge across request storage and backups (subject to retention windows). For ephemeral mode there's nothing to delete, but for stored mode we will run the purge and return an audit ticket.
[05:58] [00:05:58] Speaker 2: (overlap) — do you support regex across nested JSON payloads?
[06:03] Liam O'Connor: Yep — rules support JSONPath selectors and regex, plus ML detectors for free text fields.
[06:10] Priya Singh: Demo time — show the console toggle for request-storage off.
[06:14] Liam O'Connor: (screen share) In Console > Routes > /payments we open the route config, toggle Request storage = Off, and hit Save. From there, new calls have header x-redwood-store: false by default. For existing routes you can run a migration to drop stored payloads.
[06:32] Daniel Kwan: When you flip that toggle, does it immediately block writes or does it wait for an in-flight grace period?
[06:38] Liam O'Connor: It's immediate for new requests. For in-flight requests, we complete the operation but mark them for deferred ejection if they're in the buffer. We also expose a "flush" action to clear the buffer on demand.
[06:49] Priya Singh: Can we demo a redaction rule?
[06:52] Liam O'Connor: Creating one now: name = Ember-Account-Regex, selector = $.payment.account_number, regex = (\d{4}-\d{4}-\d{4}), action = mask (last 4). Save. Now run a sample request.
[07:09] [00:07:10] (API POST sample shown)
[07:15] System: Request received (masked in logs) — redaction rule matched, masked value = ****-****-1234.
[07:22] Aisha Roberts: Nice — can we make it remove entirely instead of mask?
[07:26] Liam O'Connor: Yes, change action to "eject_field" and it will remove the JSON key before persisting. Note that changes how the model sees the prompt — if you need model context, use mask instead.
[07:38] Daniel Kwan: Any way to test redaction rules safely in prod without affecting users?
[07:42] Liam O'Connor: Console has a "dry run" mode that simulates rules and shows counts/hits but doesn't persist changes. You can also run in a QA org.
[07:52] Priya Singh: Suppose we want token-level suppression that removes just names but keeps grammar — will that break model quality?
[07:59] Liam O'Connor: Masking names with placeholders preserves grammar and usually keeps quality intact. Fully removing tokens can reduce context and sometimes increase hallucinations — that's part of the tradeoff we'll measure in the pilot.
[08:12] Maya Chen: Quick interjection — on Optimize, we can suggest redaction configs that minimize quality loss while hitting compliance targets. It looks at your prompt patterns and suggests which fields to mask vs eject.
[08:23] Priya Singh: Is that the "Optimize" product? We haven't seen that.
[08:26] Liam O'Connor: Yes — Redwood Optimize. Example: it analyzed your typical payment flows and suggested only mask last 4 digits while ejecting full SSN patterns. It also provides estimated token-cost delta.
[08:36] Daniel Kwan: Can Optimize run offline against a sample dataset so we don't send live customer data?
[08:41] Maya Chen: Totally. You can upload a scrubbed prompt corpus or run a local Optimize job in Private that never leaves your VPC.
[08:51] Priya Singh: Let's talk about incident response — if there's a leakage, how do we rotate keys and ensure data isn't recoverable?
[08:58] Liam O'Connor: For customer-managed KMS we recommend rotating keys and then invoking a rekey-and-eject process. Re-encryption or key destruction can make stored backups unrecoverable; we pair that with audit tickets.
[09:10] Aisha Roberts: One compliance nuance — some regulators require ability to produce original content for audits, so we may need reversible storage for a brief period. Is that supported?
[09:18] Liam O'Connor: Yes configurable TTL for reversible mode and auditor access can be implemented with cross-org SSO + time-limited KMS grant. Everything's audited.
[09:29] [00:09:29] Priya Singh: Can we see the audit logs UI?
[09:33] Liam O'Connor: (navigates) Here, Console > Audit logs — filter by event type (redaction, ejection, key-access). Each event shows timestamp, rule id, actor, and an audit ticket link. If original was removed, the payload column shows 'REDACTED'.
[09:47] Daniel Kwan: Do logs ship to our SIEM in a way that retains the mapping to rule IDs so we can correlate?
[09:53] Liam O'Connor: Yes we emit rule IDs and hash of request ID; you can correlate without exposing payload.
[10:01] Priya Singh: A few risk items from our side: 1) We need reproducible deletion; 2) We need no PII in third-party metrics; 3) We need an SLA on the ejection job. Are those manageable?
[10:11] Maya Chen: We can commit to ejection SLAs in enterprise contracts, and all three items are supported — we'll surface them in the compliance pack.
[10:19] Aisha Roberts: About retention windows — do you support custom retention per-route?
[10:23] Liam O'Connor: Yes per-route retention windows (e.g., 0, 24h, 30d) and global org defaults.
[10:29] [00:10:29] (brief silence)
[10:33] Daniel Kwan: Performance question again — if we route PII-heavy traffic to a dedicated pool that runs redaction as a pre-step, does that reduce latency overhead?
[10:42] Liam O'Connor: It can. Dedicated pools co-locate detectors and model instances, reducing network hops. Also you can pre-process client-side to further cut latencies.
[10:50] Priya Singh: Cost considerations — does redaction add to token billing?
[10:54] Liam O'Connor: We bill tokens consumed by the model. Pre-inference ejection reduces tokens billed because fewer tokens are sent to the model. Masking doesn't typically change token count much. Optimize will estimate cost delta.
[11:06] Maya Chen: We're at the halfway mark — any other blockers?
[11:09] Priya Singh: Two more: 1) Data residency — we need EU data to stay in EU. 2) SSO and RBAC integration.
[11:16] Liam O'Connor: Data residency supported by region selection; on Private, you control the physical location. For SSO we support SAML and OIDC and fine-grained RBAC in Console.
[11:26] Aisha Roberts: Vault & HSM specifics — can we get a diagram showing where keys live?
[11:31] Maya Chen: We'll attach an architecture diagram in the follow-up email.
[11:35] Daniel Kwan: On the API flags, is there a way to default to not storing and opt-in per-request? We prefer default-off.
[11:42] Liam O'Connor: Yes set org-default to store:false and allow route-level opt-in. The default is controllable.
[11:47] Priya Singh: Let's run a quick end-to-end test: toggle route to ephemeral and send a sample payment request.
[11:51] (demo request fired)
[11:55] System: Received request, storage mode = ephemeral, no payload persisted. Telemetry event emitted: {event: "request_processed", route: "/payments", latency_ms: 87} (payload omitted)
[12:07] Priya Singh: I see the telemetry, but not the body. Exactly what we want.
[12:11] Maya Chen: Great — one note: if you need post-mortem debug, we recommend ephemeral+buffer for a short TTL with strict access controls.
[12:21] Daniel Kwan: Any limitations on file uploads or attachments? We send PDFs sometimes.
[12:26] Liam O'Connor: Attachments can be piped through the same pipeline and redaction rules can apply to text extracted by OCR; large binary objects are stored separately and subject to the same retention toggles.
[12:40] Aisha Roberts: Our audit team will want a demo of the ejection API; can Liam provide a scripted example?
[12:45] Liam O'Connor: Yep I'll include ejection API examples and sample curl in the follow-up.
[12:49] Priya Singh: What about false positives in ML detectors? We can't silence customers because of aggressive redaction.
[12:55] Liam O'Connor: You can tune sensitivity and add allow-list patterns. Also Optimize can suggest a threshold that balances recall vs precision for your corpus.
[13:07] [00:13:07] Maya Chen: Quick commercial question — any timeline constraints for pilot?
[13:12] Priya Singh: We'd like to start a pilot in early October and run 4 weeks.
[13:16] Maya Chen: Sounds good — we'll aim for provisioning the pilot tenant by 2026-10-05.
[13:22] Daniel Kwan: Billing — will trial be free or metered?
[13:25] Maya Chen: Standard trials are usage-metered with a credit; enterprise pilots can be structured. We'll propose options in the next email.
[13:33] Aisha Roberts: A quick security question — if we do reversible storage, what prevents a rogue engineer from decrypting data?
[13:40] Liam O'Connor: Access is gated by RBAC and KMS grants; key access is audited and requires time-limited elevated privileges. We can also enforce approval workflows for key operations.
[13:52] Priya Singh: Could we get an SLA for ejection job times? We may need 24-hour max on large ejections.
[13:58] Maya Chen: We'll propose SLA terms for the pilot and for enterprise contracts.
[14:05] Daniel Kwan: Any sample config for Datadog mapping?
[14:08] Liam O'Connor: Yes, I'll include a sample mapping.
[14:11] Priya Singh: Last thing — are there pre-built compliance templates for banking/finance?
[14:16] Maya Chen: We have templates for finance, healthcare, and retail. We'll include the banking template in the follow-up.
[14:22] (wrap-up)
[14:24] Maya Chen: Ok recap — we will: 1) Send SOC2 + KMS docs (Maya), 2) Provision pilot org with ephemeral default and Ember redaction profile (Liam), 3) Provide ejection API examples and Datadog mapping (Liam), 4) Ember will confirm pilot metrics and legal owner (Priya).
[14:41] Priya Singh: Thanks everyone, this was really useful. We'll follow-up internally and aim to confirm by next week.
[14:48] Maya Chen: Appreciate your time — we'll get the email out today and schedule the benchmarking slot.
[14:55] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional audio drop at 00:01:40 and 00:07:10, small mis-recognitions of product name ("Redwood Optimize" sometimes transcribed as "Redwood Optimizer"). Some filler words preserved.
